title: Emptying the sea with a blade of grass
hookLine: one blade of grass, dipped in the sea, one drop at a time, until the sea is empty. Gaudapada uses that picture for steadying the mind
carry: asparsha yoga: steady the mind, grasp at nothing
last: THE MANDUKYA KARIKA: AJATI, NO BIRTH.

lines: A BLADE OF GRASS, THE SEA.
THE PATIENCE OF STEADYING A MIND.
cards: One blade of grass. Dip its tip in the sea. Lift it.
One drop hangs there, shining, and falls onto the sand. Dip it again. Another drop.
Now keep going, without hurry and without giving up, until the sea is empty. It sounds like a riddle, or a punishment from an old story. It's neither.
It's a line from the Mandukya Karika, and Gaudapada isn't joking. He's describing how to steady a mind, and he says it takes exactly that kind of patience.

teach.h: ASPARSHA: THE YOGA OF NO CONTACT.
teach.b: It would be easy to think Gaudapada has nothing to say about practice. He does. He names a discipline asparsha yoga, the yoga of no contact, meaning no grasping, no clinging to what appears.
And he admits it's hard. Even yogis, he says, are afraid of it; they see fear where there's nothing to fear.

teach.h: THE OCEAN AND A BLADE OF GRASS.
teach.b: Then the image: the mind is to be steadied without growing weary, the way someone might empty the ocean drop by drop with the tip of a blade of grass. The point isn't that the task can be finished by Tuesday.
It's the kind of effort: tireless, unhurried, not discouraged. Then he gets specific, almost like a coach.

teach.h: WAKE IT, CALM IT, NOTICE, LEAVE IT.
teach.b: When the mind drifts toward dullness and sleep, wake it. When it's scattered, bring it back to calm. When it's caught in desire, know that it's caught.
When it's resting in balance, don't disturb it.
And a warning that surprises some readers: don't sit and savor the happiness that comes in deep stillness. Stay unattached, through clear seeing. Even the sweet part isn't something to grab.

This fits the rest of the Karika. If nothing is truly born, the practice isn't building something new. It's the patient undoing of grasping, until the mind, in his words elsewhere, stops imagining and comes to rest.
This is dhyana, meditation, as Gaudapada teaches it: not one heroic sitting that empties the mind, but coming back, again and again, without weariness.
His instructions are humble ones: wake it, calm it, notice it, leave it be.

how: In Advaita Vedanta, meditation is practiced alongside study and reflection, and Gaudapada's verses on steadying the mind are read as guidance for it.

practice: Try Gaudapada's four small moves. If the mind gets drowsy, sit up a little and open your attention; if it scatters, come back to one breath.
If it reaches for something, a plan or a craving, just notice: caught; and if it rests, let it rest, without holding on to the rest. If you pray, let each return be an offering.

wordCard.voice: The Mandukya Karika. Gaudapada's verses on the Mandukya Upanishad, with their patient practice: steadying the mind like emptying the ocean with a blade of grass.

orig.note: Sanskrit: no contact, no touching; Gaudapada's name for his yoga of non-grasping.
